title_en: On the Soul, Against the Arians
author: Eustathius of Antioch
occasion: Eustathius writes against Arian claims that Christ assumed a body without a human soul. He argues from Christ's birth, growth, suffering, death, and resurrection that he possessed a real human body with a soul, and specifically that Christ's soul led the thief's soul into paradise, proving the soul's distinct reality and continued existence apart from the body.
argument: Eustathius argues that Christ took a complete human nature, including a human soul, against Arian teaching that the Word assumed a soulless body. He points to Christ's infancy, growth, and the physical marks of his passion and resurrection—the wounds, the pierced side, the nail prints, the blood, the signs of death—as evidence of bodily reality. He contends that the Arians deny Christ a soul in order to attribute the changes and passions to the divine Spirit, so as to persuade people that what is changeable could not be born from the unchangeable nature, thereby denying the Son's generation from the Father's unchangeable nature. Finally, he uses the promise to the thief on the cross to show that Christ's human soul, united to the Word, led the thief's soul into paradise while Christ's body still lay in the tomb.

outline.move: Eustathius appeals to Christ's infancy, growth, miracles, wounds, death, and bodily resurrection as proof of his real human life.

He states that the tabernacle of the Word and God is not the same thing as that through which the blessed Stephen beheld the divine glory, and argues that Christ foretold his bodily death and after rising showed his wounded body, showing that if Christ had not voluntarily surrendered his body to death, this would attach great weakness to him.

He explains that the Arians deny Christ a soul in order to attribute his passions to the divine Spirit and persuade people that what is changeable could not be born from the unchangeable nature, and he cites Jeremiah as introducing God's voices, through which he shows that God does not accept the prayers of the righteous if they should wish to intercede on behalf of murderers.

He argues that Christ's soul, united to the Word, led the thief's soul into paradise on the day of the crucifixion while Christ's body remained in the tomb, proving the soul's distinct reality and continued existence apart from the body.

scripture: The author cites the Septuagint, using Greek forms of Old Testament names (Mōysēs, Samouēl, Hieremias). Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint. Citations should be given in modern form with LXX book names where they differ from the Hebrew.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He argues from Christ's birth, growth, suffering, death, and resurrection that he possessed a real human body with a soul
_unresolved_facts.fix: He argues from Christ's birth, growth, suffering, death, and resurrection that he possessed a real human body; the argument for the soul's distinct reality comes primarily from the thief on the cross in section 17

_unresolved_facts.claim: He points to Christ's infancy, growth, and the physical marks of his passion and resurrection—the wounds, the pierced side, the nail prints, the blood, the signs of death—as evidence of bodily reality
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἵνα δὲ παρῶ λέγειν τὰς ἐπὶ ἐδάφους ἐκπληρωθείσας θαυματουργίας
_unresolved_facts.fix: He points to Christ's infancy, growth, and the physical marks of his passion and resurrection as evidence of bodily reality; notably, he explicitly passes over (παρῶ) discussing the miracles performed on earth

_unresolved_facts.claim: He contends that the Arians deny Christ a soul in order to attribute the changes and passions to the divine Spirit, so as to persuade people that what is changeable could not be born from the unchangeable nature, thereby denying the Son's generation from the Father's unchangeable nature
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἵνα εἰ δυνηθεῖεν ὑποφθεῖραί τινας, ταῦθ' οὕτως ἔχειν ὁρίζεσθαι, τηνικαῦτα τὰς τῶν παθῶν ἀλλοιώσεις τῷ θείῳ περιάψαντες Πνεύματι, ῥᾳδίως ἀναπείσωσιν αὐτοὺς, ὡς οὐκ ἔστι τὸ τρεπτὸν ἐκ τῆς ἀτρέπτου φύσεως γεννηθέν
_unresolved_facts.fix: He contends that the Arians deny Christ a soul in order to attribute the changes and passions to the divine Spirit, so as to persuade people that what is changeable could not be born from the unchangeable nature; the text does not explicitly connect this to denying the Son's generation from the Father's unchangeable nature

_unresolved_facts.claim: He states that the tabernacle of the Word and God is not the same thing as that through which the blessed Stephen beheld the divine glory
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὐ γὰρ ταὐτόν ἐστιν ἡ σκηνὴ τοῦ Λόγου καὶ Θεοῦ, δι' ἧς τὴν θείαν ἐθεώρει δόξαν ὁ μακάριος Στέφανος
_unresolved_facts.fix: He states that the tabernacle of the Word and God is the same thing as that through which the blessed Stephen beheld the divine glory (ταὐτόν = 'the same', not 'not the same'; the οὐ negates the sentence as a whole, meaning 'For it is not the case that the tabernacle of the Word and God is not the same as that through which...' i.e., it IS the same)

_unresolved_facts.claim: and argues that Christ foretold his bodily death and after rising showed his wounded body, showing that if Christ had not voluntarily surrendered his body to death, this would attach great weakness to him
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Πρῶτον μὲν πολλὴν αὐτῷ περιάπτουσιν ἀδυναμίαν, ὅτι μὴ οἷός τ' ἐγένετο τὴν τῶν πολεμίων ὁρμὴν ἐπισχεῖν
_unresolved_facts.fix: and argues that Christ foretold his bodily death and after rising showed his wounded body; he then states that if Christ had not voluntarily surrendered his body to death, the Arians would first of all attach great weakness to him, that he was not able to check the onrush of his enemies

_unresolved_facts.claim: and he cites Jeremiah as introducing God's voices, through which he shows that God does not accept the prayers of the righteous if they should wish to intercede on behalf of murderers
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Σύμφωνα δὲ τούτοις διεξιὼν ὁ αὐτὸς Ἱερεμίας εἰσηγεῖται τὰς τοῦ Θεοῦ διακονούμενος φωνάς, δι' ὧν δείκνυσιν, ὅτι μήτε τὰς τῶν δικαίων προσίεται πρεσβείας, εἰ βουληθεῖεν τῶν μιαιφόνων χάριν ἀξιῶσαι
_unresolved_facts.fix: and he cites Jeremiah as introducing the voices of God which he serves, through which he shows that God does not accept the prayers of the righteous if they should wish to intercede on behalf of murderers; the connection of this citation to the anti-Arian argument about Christ's soul is not explicitly explained in the fragment

_unresolved_facts.claim: The blessed Stephen, who beheld the divine glory
_unresolved_facts.fix: The blessed Stephen, who beheld the divine glory through the tabernacle of the Word and God

_unresolved_facts.claim: Introduced as Jeremiah introducing the voices of God which he serves, through which he shows; the quotation is introduced with 'And the Lord said to me, saying'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ εἶπε Κύριος πρός με λέγων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The quotation is introduced with 'And the Lord said to me, saying' (Καὶ εἶπε Κύριος πρός με λέγων); Jeremiah is described as 'introducing the voices of God which he serves' (εἰσηγεῖται τὰς τοῦ Θεοῦ διακονούμενος φωνάς), not 'introducing the voices of God which he serves, through which he shows'
